metadata.title: When Does an AI Handoff Actually Finish?
metadata.topic: AI TOOL HANDOFF · WORKING WITH CLAUDE
metadata.purpose: Answer whether a task handed to Claude is done the moment it comes back, or only once a human confirms it. Lands the carry-out that the handoff finishes with a human signature, not with delivery.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carried unfilled '>' template placeholders at every skill-specific fact, and its named source_skill file does not exist on this machine -- see QUESTION.md. This redo reconstructs a generic, defensible AI-tool-handoff account from the title/family rather than lifting facts that were never written.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the redlined contract page: marked-not-accepted, then signed-final)

beats.narration_text: Someone hands Claude a contract redline and calls the job finished the second it comes back. Wrong verb. What just finished is the drafting — the handoff itself hasn't started yet. Liam, in for Bear.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Can I just have Claude finish this contract redline?', hesitates on 'finish', corrects to 'start', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('finish' -> 'start') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening when you treat delivery as completion. The instruction reads 'redline every use of the word Vendor.' You meant one specific vendor. Claude does not know that — it does what the string says, not what you meant. Every 'Vendor' gets marked, precisely, at high speed. The execution is flawless. The contract is now wrong. Nothing in the loop was tasked with catching the gap between what you asked for and what you meant, so nothing did.

shot.new_visual_element: A contract page; every instance of one word gets marked, cleanly and correctly; a caption reveals the instruction itself was the error

production_viz.label: Flawless execution, wrong instruction
production_viz.mechanic: A contract page with several instances of the word 'Vendor' highlighted one by one, each cleanly struck and replaced -- fast, precise, correct to the letter of the instruction. Once all instances are marked, a caption fades in below: 'only one of these should have changed.' The page's border flashes accent, not from an error in the marks, but from the instruction itself.

beats.narration_text: A handoff that actually works ships with three parts, and each one exists to catch a different failure mode. Scope: exactly what's being asked — narrow enough that 'did it do the thing' is a real question with a yes or no answer. Boundary: the point where a human has to say yes before anything counts as final — that's the pause the last example didn't have. Record: what changed, marked in the margin, so the check is fast instead of a cold re-read. Watch the anchor. That same contract redline comes back from Claude with every changed clause marked. Not accepted. Marked. Those are different states, and the whole design turns on the difference.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- three labeled parts lighting in turn (scope / boundary / record), then a redlined contract page stamped MARKED -- NOT ACCEPTED

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- three parts, then the marked page
production_viz.mechanic: Three chips fade in one at a time across the top, each labelled with a part of a working handoff (scope / boundary / record), then fade out together. THE ANCHOR. A contract page appears, its margin carrying several clause marks in accent color, with a stamp across the corner reading 'MARKED -- NOT ACCEPTED' in bold. THIS EXACT PAGE RETURNS, SIGNED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The lawyer opens the same redline, checks the margin against the record instead of re-reading the whole contract cold, and only then does it become final. That is what the boundary is for — the finish is the signature, not the delivery. Two failure modes this design deliberately rules out. Silence is not approval: if nobody looked, nothing was signed, no matter how long the document sat there. And heavy rewriting is not failure: a clean first pass and one that gets torn up can both be the handoff working exactly as intended, because the point was never for Claude to be right the first time — it was for a human to decide what final means.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the marked page gets a human signature stamp and becomes FINAL; then splits into 'silence is not approval' and 'rewritten is not failure'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- marked, then signed
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CONTRACT PAGE RETURNS, identical placement, its 'MARKED -- NOT ACCEPTED' stamp crossed out and replaced with a hand-drawn signature mark and a new stamp reading 'FINAL'. It splits into two cards: left reads 'no comments' with a struck-through 'APPROVED' beneath it labelled 'silence is not approval'; right reads 'heavily rewritten' with a checkmark beneath it labelled 'rewritten is not failure'.

beats.narration_text: Here's what actually finishes the handoff. Not Claude's delivery. A person signing off on what came back.

props.quote: The handoff finishes with a signature — not a delivery.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read the prompt with me. Take one document you're already reviewing. Ask Claude to make exactly one change — a single clause, a single term. When it comes back, check the marked change against your instruction line by line before you accept anything. That is the whole handoff in miniature: one scope, one boundary, one signature. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Take one document I'm reviewing right now. Make exactly one change -- a single clause, a single term -- so I can check the marked change against my instruction before accepting anything.

beats.narration_text: Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It walks any frontier model through building you a scope, a boundary, and a record for a real task you are about to hand off — the same three parts we just took apart. Read it once, drop it in, answer the question it asks back, and you get a checklist you can use tomorrow. Go deeper: what failure mode does each part of that handoff catch, and which failure mode has no catch in your workflow right now?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to design an AI handoff I can trust in my own workflow. I am about to hand a task to a large language model — writing, analysis, editing, or research — and I need to know when the task is actually finished versus just delivered. Walk me through the three parts of a working handoff for MY specific task: (1) the scope I should ask for, narrow enough that 'did it do the thing' has a yes or no answer; (2) the boundary — the specific check I run before anything counts as final; (3) the record — what the model should hand me back so I can verify quickly instead of re-reading everything cold. Ask me what the task is, then give me a scope-boundary-record checklist tailored to it.
